captions.text: In 1786, Benjamin Franklin printed a map of a river inside the ocean.
Today, waves roll onto a Florida beach. Something shiny washes in.
It's as wide as a cookie, and shaped like a heart.
A seed? From across the ocean?
It grew in a giant pod on a rainforest vine, far to the south.
It fell into a river, then rode the ocean currents for months.
Some sea hearts even sail to the beaches of Scotland.
How can one plant start new plants so far away?

words: To make new living things of the same kind. Plants reproduce to keep their kind going.
When pollen moves from one flower to another flower of the same kind, so seeds can form.
A powdery material made by flowers. Pollen must travel to another flower to help make seeds.
A plant part that can grow into a whole new plant. Seeds form after pollination.
A tiny cell that can grow into a new plant. Ferns and mosses use spores instead of seeds.
An animal that carries pollen from flower to flower. Bees, butterflies, and hummingbirds are pollinators.

parts.title: Plants Need to Make New Plants
parts.html:
When a plant reproduces, it makes new plants just like itself. Without reproduction, plants would eventually disappear.

Some plants reproduce using seeds. Others, like ferns and mosses, reproduce using spores. Both are ways of starting a new life.

parts.title: Flowers, Pollen, and Pollinators
parts.html:
Many plants grow flowers. Flowers make a powdery material called pollen. For seeds to form, pollen has to travel from one flower to another. That is pollination.

Wind can carry pollen, but animals do most of the work. Bees, butterflies, and hummingbirds are pollinators. They pick up pollen while they feed, then drop it off at the next flower.

parts.title: Seeds, Spores, and Getting Around
parts.html:
After pollination, many plants form seeds. Seeds need to get away from the parent plant to find space to grow. They travel by wind, water, animals, and even gravity.

Ferns don't make flowers or seeds at all. They release tiny spores from the undersides of their leaves. The spores drift through the air, and some grow into new ferns.

compare.title: Does a seed's shape match the way it travels?
compare.look: Two real seeds, each on a lit specimen tray. Specimen A is a maple seed with a thin, papery wing. Specimen B is a sea heart, the seed from our film. Under the trays are two things for a test: an electric fan and a tub of water.

trays.label: Specimen A

trays.alt: Two shiny brown sea heart seeds
trays.label: Specimen B

ask.q: Which seed has a thin, papery wing?
ask.ok: Yes. Specimen A, the maple seed, has a wing.
ask.miss: Look closely. Which seed looks like a helicopter blade?

ask.q: Which seed is hard, round, and shiny?
ask.ok: Yes. Specimen B, the sea heart, is hard and shiny.
ask.miss: Look again. Which one is shaped like a heart?

compare.testDo: Put the fan by one tray and the tub of water by the other: drag them, or tap each one, then tap a tray. Press Test it. Then swap them and press it again.
compare.disclaimer: This is a model. It shows what really happens to these seeds, sped up.

Afan.text: The maple seed spun like a helicopter and drifted far across the room.

Awater.text: The maple seed sat on the water and didn't go anywhere. Its wing is made for wind. Try the fan here.

Bfan.text: The fan couldn't move the heavy sea heart at all. Try the water here.

Bwater.text: The sea heart floated! It has a hollow space inside, so water can carry it far away.

compare.frame: This seed has ___, so it travels by ___.

curator.A: Wing → wind. A maple seed spins as it falls, so the wind can carry it away from the parent tree.
curator.B: Floats → water. A sea heart can float for months, so rivers and ocean currents carry it to faraway beaches.

compare.missFeat: Look at {label} again. Does it have a wing, or is it a hard seed that floats?
compare.missClaim: Think about your test. Which seed flew, and which one floated?
compare.done: A seed's shape helps it travel. Wings ride the wind. Seeds that float ride the water. Either way, the new plant grows far from its parent.

after.kicker: 🎬 Behind the scenes · Seeds don't just drop
after.alt: A coconut that washed up between big rocks, with a new green palm shoot growing out of it
after.html: This coconut floated in the sea, washed up between rocks, and sprouted a new palm. If every seed dropped right under its parent, the young plants would crowd together and fight for light and water. Seeds that travel get room to grow.

wall.look: A cutaway (a slice) of a lily flower, from the outside in. It is a model, with a real close-up photo for each level. Each level is one part of the flower, and each part has a job in making seeds. The brass dial on the left shows how deep inside the flower you are.

predict.q: Where in a flower do you think seeds start to grow?
options: Deep inside, at the bottom of the flower
On the outside of the petals
predict.mine: Your prediction: {p}. Let's ride down the flower and find out.
predict.confirm: You predicted deep inside. The evidence agrees: seeds start in the seed room at the bottom of the flower.
predict.change: You predicted the petals. The evidence changed that idea: seeds start deep inside, in the seed room.

wall.skyAlt: A white Easter lily in bloom, with a small insect visiting it
wall.skyCap: A real lily with a pollinator visiting · Alabama
wall.locked: Brush the level above first. The elevator goes down, one level at a time.
wall.first: Brush the glowing top layer. Drag across it (or tap it again and again).
wall.next: Going deeper into the flower. Brush Level {n}.
wall.endText: Look at the line. The petals on the outside invite pollinators. Pollen holders and the sticky tip pass pollen along. Deep inside, the seed room is where new seeds begin.
wall.rule: Every part of a flower helps make seeds. Petals invite pollinators, pollen holders make pollen, the sticky tip catches it, and the seed room grows the seeds.

mix.q: Does every plant have flowers and a seed room like this lily?

options.miss: Not every plant! Ferns and mosses have no flowers and no seeds. What do they make instead?

options.t: No. Ferns and mosses make spores instead.
options.ok: Yes! Ferns and mosses have no flowers and no seeds. They make spores, tiny cells that drift away and grow into new plants.

wow.title: Seeds that sail the sea
wow.alt: A huge, twisting sea heart vine (monkey ladder) arching over a garden path
wow.caption: A sea heart vine, also called monkey ladder, in a garden in Hawaii.
wow.html:
Sea hearts grow on giant vines in tropical forests. Their pods can grow longer than you are tall! Each seed has a hollow space inside, so it floats.

When the seeds fall into rivers, they wash out to sea. Some ride the Gulf Stream for a year or more and land on beaches in Florida, and even Scotland and Norway. Long ago, people in Scotland found them and called them Molucca beans.
wow.insetCap: Sea heart seeds, about as wide as a cookie.

keyIdea: Plants reproduce: they make new plants of the same kind. Flowering plants often use pollination and seeds. Ferns and mosses use spores instead. Either way, the goal is the same: new life.

quiz.q: What does it mean when a plant reproduces?

options.t: It makes new plants of the same kind
options.ok: 🌱 That's right! Reproduction means making new living things of the same kind. It keeps the plant's kind going.

options.miss: Think about what the word "reproduce" means. What is the plant trying to make?
Think about what the word "reproduce" means. What is the plant trying to make?

quiz.q: After a bee carries pollen from flower to flower, what can happen next?

options.miss: Think about what happens after pollination. What can the flower make?

options.ok: 🌸 Exactly! Pollination, when pollen moves from one flower to another, is what makes seeds possible for many flowering plants.

options.t: The pollen melts in the rain
options.miss: Think about what happens after pollination. What can the flower make?

quiz.q: Which plant uses spores to reproduce instead of seeds?

options.miss: Apple and maple trees both make seeds. Which plant has no flowers and no seeds?
Apple and maple trees both make seeds. Which plant has no flowers and no seeds?

options.ok: 🌿 Yes! Ferns don't make flowers or seeds. They release tiny spores from the undersides of their fronds, and if a spore lands in the right spot, a new fern grows.

partA.title: Read the cases
partA.do: Read each one. Pick the best answer, or type your answer.

items.q: Case A: A bee lands on a flower, picks up yellow pollen, then flies to a second flower of the same kind. What is moving?

options.ok: Yes. The bee carries pollen from flower to flower. That's pollination.

options.miss: The bee is carrying yellow powder. What is it called?
Spores come from ferns and mosses, not flowers. What yellow powder do flowers make?

items.q: Case B: A maple tree drops a winged seed. It spins like a helicopter as the wind carries it 30 feet away. What is moving?

options.miss: This part has a wing and can grow into a new tree. What is it?

options.ok: Yes. The wind carries the maple's winged seed away from the parent tree.

options.miss: Maples are flowering trees. They make seeds, not spores.

items.q: Case C: A fern in a shady corner releases tiny brown dots from the undersides of its fronds. They drift away on the breeze. What is moving?

options.miss: Ferns have no flowers, so they don't make pollen. What do ferns make?
Ferns have no seeds. What tiny cells do they release?

options.ok: Yes. Ferns release spores, and the wind carries them to new places.

items.q: Case D: A bird eats a bright berry, flies two miles away, and drops the seeds in its droppings. A new bush sprouts there. What is moving?

options.ok: Yes. The bird carries the berry's seeds inside its body to a new place.

options.miss: A new bush sprouted. What plant part grows into a new plant?
Berry bushes are flowering plants. What do their berries hold?
